paragraphs.heading: What a carboxylic acid is
paragraphs.text: A carboxylic acid is a polar organic acid that holds a carboxyl group, −C(=O)−OH, joined to an R-group. The carboxyl group is a hydroxyl group and a carbonyl group acting together as one unit. The general formula is usually written R−COOH or R−CO₂H, where R can be an organyl group, such as an alkyl or aryl group, or simply hydrogen.

paragraphs.heading: A common but weak acid
paragraphs.text: Carboxylic acids are Brønsted–Lowry acids, which means they give away protons, H⁺. They are the most common kind of organic acid, yet they are often counted as weak acids, since in water only part of them splits into ions. Losing the proton leaves a carboxylate anion. That anion is stabilized by resonance, with its negative charge spread across the two oxygen atoms.

paragraphs.heading: Names ending in -ic and -oic
paragraphs.text: Carboxylic acids are commonly known by trivial names, which often end in -ic acid. The IUPAC naming system uses the ending -oic acid instead, so butyric acid, CH₃CH₂CH₂CO₂H, is officially butanoic acid. The carboxylate anion usually takes the ending -ate, so the anion of acetic acid is acetate.

paragraphs.heading: Mixing with water
paragraphs.text: Small carboxylic acids, with 1 to 5 carbons, dissolve in water. Bigger ones dissolve poorly, because their longer alkyl chains are more and more hydrophobic, and they mix better with less polar solvents such as ethers and alcohols. Even hydrophobic carboxylic acids react with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give sodium salts that dissolve in water. Enanthic acid, for instance, dissolves in water only to 0.2 g/L, while its sodium salt dissolves readily.

paragraphs.heading: Why they boil so high
paragraphs.text: Carboxylic acids tend to boil at higher temperatures than water. One reason is their larger surface area; another is that pairs of molecules cling together through hydrogen bonds, forming stable dimers. To boil, the liquid must either break those bonds or carry off each pair whole, which sharply raises the energy needed to vaporize it. In nonpolar surroundings these acids usually exist as such pairs.

paragraphs.heading: Smell and detection
paragraphs.text: Carboxylic acids often have strong, sour smells, while their esters tend to smell fruity and pleasant, and many esters go into perfume. Infrared spectroscopy picks carboxylic acids out easily. They show a sharp band from the C=O bond between 1680 and 1725 cm⁻¹, along with a broad O–H band in the 2500 to 3000 cm⁻¹ range.

paragraphs.heading: In life and industry
paragraphs.text: Carboxylic acids are common in nature and are also made in large amounts by industry. Amino acids and fatty acids are key examples, and soaps are important carboxylate salts. Most of the material in lipids is esters of fatty acids, and most of the material in proteins is polyamides built from aminocarboxylic acids. In photosynthesis, the protein RuBisCo, the most abundant protein of all, drives the carbon-fixation step that yields carboxylic acids. Industry uses them to make polymers, pharmaceuticals, solvents and food additives.
